# Gestational Weight Gain and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy with Prepregnancy and Early Pregnancy GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Exposure

**Authors:** Nishita Pondugula; Jennifer F. Culhane; Lisbet S. Lundsberg; Caitlin Partridge; Audrey A. Merriam

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Sciences, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT

## Abstract

To evaluate the association between peripregnancy GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) exposure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) and gestational weight gain (GWG).

We conducted a retrospective cohort study including all patients delivering between 2014-2024 with GLP-1RA exposure up to one year before pregnancy. Participants were identified through electronic medical record (EMR) query with manual medical record abstraction to confirm exposure stop dates. GLP-1RA exposure was classified by indication: pregestational diabetes mellitus (PGDM) or weight management (WM). Unexposed control groups for each indication cohort were identified from a 2021-2022 existing institutional data repository. Demographic and clinical characteristics and obstetric outcomes were compared. The two primary outcomes were GWG and HDP. GWG was quantified as below, meeting, or exceeding recommended GWG. Crude and adjusted odds ratios were estimated using multivariable modeling. Regression analysis was stratified as GLP-1RA exposure prepregnancy only or during pregnancy.

We included 243 patients who were GLP-1RA exposed up to one year prior to pregnancy with 65.4% with evidence of use during pregnancy. Overall, 103 (42.4%) patients used GLP-1RA for PGDM and 140 (57.6%) for WM, and were compared with 175 PGDM unexposed controls and 200 WM unexposed controls (n=100 BMI between 30<40 kg/m2; n=100 BMI ≥40 kg/m2).

GLP-1RA exposure was not associated with GWG in the PGDM cohort but was associated with decreased odds of GWG below recommendations (aOR 0.38 (95% CI 0.18-0.80)) in the WM cohort. GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of HDP when compared with unexposed controls with PGDM (aOR 0.52 (95% CI 0.30-0.90)) and with unexposed controls undergoing WM (aOR=0.51 (0.30-0.87)). These associations were slightly more robust among patients exposed during pregnancy.

In individuals undergoing WM, peripregnancy GLP-1RA exposure was associated with decreased risk of GWG below recommendations, which may reflect rebound weight gain after cessation. Peripregnancy GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of developing HDP for both PGDM and WM cohorts. Additional studies are needed to guide GLP-1RA use in pregnancy and to better elucidate any risks of exposure.

## Abstract

Prepregnancy and early pregnancy GLP-1 receptor agonist use was associated with a reduction in gestational weight gain below recommendations and lower risk of developing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.

## Introduction:

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use has rapidly increased for treatment of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity.1,2 Weight loss increases spontaneous pregnancy rates, and the prevalence of exposure to GLP-1RAs in the peripregnancy period, including early gestation, is increasing.3–6 Case reports and observational human studies show no increased risk of congenital malformations or adverse pregnancy outcomes after prepregnancy or early pregnancy GLP-1RA exposure.5,7–9 However, based on concerns of fetal death and congenital abnormalities in animal studies, GLP-1RA prescribing information recommends discontinuation two months prior to pregnancy due to the medication’s long washout period.7,10,11

In non-pregnant adults, GLP-1RAs are associated with weight reduction and improved cardiovascular health. GLP-1RAs lead to decreased incidence of death, stroke, and myocardial infarction and are associated with blood pressure lowering effects.12–15 Prepregnancy weight loss, through lifestyle modifications or bariatric surgery, is associated with a reduction in hypertension and HDP.16,17,18

Little is known about the effect of GLP-1RAs on gestational weight gain (GWG) or HDP. This study aimed to evaluate the association between GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy and in early pregnancy and both GWG and HDP.

## Methods:

We conducted a retrospective cohort study that received Yale University Institutional Review Board approval with a waiver for informed consent. All patients with a delivery admission encounter between 2014-2024 in one large medical center with four delivery hospitals and GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy were identified through an electronic medical record (EMR) query with manual medical record abstraction to confirm exposure and to ascertain medication stop date relative to ‘conception’. We used calculated dates of ‘conception’ to denote timing of GLP-1RA exposure as ‘prepregnancy’ or ‘during pregnancy’. Timing of conception was calculated based on clinical gestational age and estimated date of delivery (EDD). In the institutional data repository, the EDD, determined clinically by the attending obstetrician from last menstrual period and/or ultrasound(s) during pregnancy, is obtained from a data table called ‘Obstetric Dating History’ in the EMR. If absent, which was rare, the EMR was searched for the EDD most proximal to delivery. For the GLP-1RA exposed cohort with data manually abstracted, the clinical gestational age most proximal to delivery was recorded. Timing of conception was considered to be two weeks after the first day of the last menstrual period. Individuals with spontaneous or induced abortions early in gestation who did not have a delivery admission were excluded. Multiple gestations were also excluded.

The primary exposure was GLP-1RA use up to one year prior to pregnancy with end dates either prepregnancy or during pregnancy. GLP-1RA exposure was confirmed via prescription data in the EMR, and manual abstraction confirmed the medication type and exact stop dates for each case based on prescription data marking end of medication prescription dispensation or, if available, date when patient was marked as no longer taking the medication in the EMR. Subcutaneous injectable GLP-1RAs in this study included dulaglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, and albiglutide. The only oral GLP-1RA included was semaglutide. Additionally, an injectable dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 receptor co-agonist, tirzepatide, was included as an exposure to GLP-1RA.

GLP-1RA exposed patients were classified according to GLP-1RA indication for use: 1) pregestational diabetes mellitus (PGDM) or 2) weight management (WM) for elevated BMI. Individuals exposed to GLP-1RA with PGDM included those with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Unexposed control groups for each indication cohort were identified from 2021-2022 delivery EMR data from an existing institutional obstetric data repository. This repository includes standardized and templated data fields including recorded diagnoses (ICD-10 codes) and billing codes (CPT). Extensive quality checks are employed including manual abstraction to minimize missingness and optimize accuracy. GLP-1RA exposure was not recorded in the institutional obstetric data repository and thus required an additional EMR query followed by manual medical record abstraction, whereas the institutional obstetric database was utilized for additional variables of interest and to identify unexposed controls. As deliveries recorded in the institutional data repository ended in January 2023 at the time of this study and the majority of cases identified who were exposed to GLP-1RAs were also from 2021-2022, we utilized the sampling timeframe of 2021-2022 to identify the unexposed control group. For exposed participants who delivered after January 2023, all variables contained in the obstetric database were manually abstracted to align with the institutional data repository utilized for unexposed controls.

PGDM controls were all patients with pregestational diabetes type I or type II managed with medication other than GLP-1RA up to one year prior to pregnancy within this timeframe. WM controls were selected using a stratified random sample of patients without PGDM not on antihyperglycemic medication up to one year prior to pregnancy with BMIs between 30<40 kg/m2 (n=100) and ≥40 kg/m2 (n=100).

The two primary outcomes in this study were GWG and HDP. Pre-pregnancy BMI and total GWG were abstracted manually from the EMR for all patients with GLP-1RA exposure. Pre-pregnancy BMI and GWG were obtained from the institutional data repository for all unexposed controls, and when these variables were missing, additional manual medical record abstraction was performed. Categories for GWG were determined by weight gain appropriate for patient’s pre-pregnancy BMI according to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) weight gain recommendations for pregnancy,19 and also accounting for gestational age at delivery following methodology by Woolfolk et al.20 Each participant’s total gestational weight gain was determined by subtracting pre-pregnancy weight from weight just prior to delivery and was compared with the normal weight gain range for their BMI and gestational age. GWG was then categorized as ‘met IOM recommendations,’ ‘below IOM recommendations,’ or ‘exceeded IOM recommendations.’

HDP was defined as gestational hypertension (gHTN), preeclampsia with or without severe features, superimposed preeclampsia, eclampsia, or hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome.21 Presence of HDP was recorded if any of these diagnoses were present as identified via International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 codes in the institutional data repository (Appendix 1, available online at http://links.lww.com/xxx).

Demographic and clinical characteristics collected include maternal age at delivery, insurance type (public, private, and none, other, self-pay), parity, race and ethnicity (Asian, Black, Hispanic, White, None of the Above), and pre-pregnancy BMI. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosis and chronic hypertension (cHTN) diagnoses were identified via ICD-10 codes (Appendix 1, available online at http://links.lww.com/xxx). Race and ethnicity were included in this study because important racial disparities have been identified related to GLP-1RA prescribing as well as in HDP, which were important inequities to be aware of and to identify if present in our population in order to adjust for the potential confounder due to racism and target subsequent quality assessment or improvement efforts to thoroughly evaluate and intervene. If a patient indicated Hispanic ethnicity, they were assigned to Hispanic ethnicity. For patients indicating Black/African American race alone or in any combination, and non-Hispanic ethnicity, patients were assigned to this category of Black/African American non-Hispanic. The method was similar for patients reporting Asian race, non-Hispanic. Other race and ethnicity included patients reporting race as unknown, do not see race, missing, Native American or Alaska Native.

Secondary obstetric outcomes included large for gestational age (LGA), fetal growth restriction (FGR), preterm birth, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) diagnosis, fetal death, insulin use during pregnancy, and metformin use during pregnancy. LGA was defined as birth weight equal to or more than the 90th percentile for a given gestational age.22 FGR was identified via ICD-10 code (Appendix 1, available online at http://links.lww.com/xxx). Preterm birth was defined as birth between 20 0/7 weeks to 36 6/7 weeks of gestation.23 Fetal death as opposed to neonatal death or livebirth was identified via EMR review primarily through the ‘Delivery Summary Activity’ sheet in Epic with potential other sources including cases in which death date and time was populated or dispensation was noted as ‘deceased’.

Continuous variables were converted into categorical variables for analysis. Baseline characteristics were compared using the appropriate bivariate test, Chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests with p<.05 considered statistically significant. Multinomial logistic regression assessed the crude (cOR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for GWG, with ‘met IOM recommendations’ as the reference, and multivariable logistic regression estimated an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) for the development of HDP, adjusting for covariates significant at p<.05 in bivariate tests or based on clinical relevance. Chronic hypertension was determined to be clinically relevant and included in all models for hypertension. Participants for whom the outcome variable was missing were excluded from regression analysis. Analyses were repeated after GLP-1RA exposure was further classified as prepregnancy only or during early pregnancy. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).

## Results:

Overall, 289 patients were identified through initial EMR query with GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy and/or during pregnancy with 53 patients delivering between 2014-2020, 57 patients delivering between 2021-2022, and 179 patients delivering in 2023-June 2024. We excluded 46 patients after manual abstraction of the EMR because GLP-1RA use did not occur up to a year before pregnancy or during pregnancy (n=39) or the pregnancy was a multiple gestation (n=7). The final cohort included 243 patients with confirmed GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy (Figure 1). Of these, 103 were exposed for an indication of PGDM with 9 who had a diagnosis of type 1 DM and the remainder who were diagnosed with type 2 DM, and 140 for WM. There were 84 (34.6%) individuals with prepregnancy only GLP-1RA exposure, while 159 (65.4%) participants had some GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy. Of those who used GLP-1RAs for PGDM, 34 (33.0%) had prepregnancy only GLP-1RA exposure and 69 (67.0%) had exposure during pregnancy. Of those who used GLP-1RAs for WM, 50 (35.7%) used GLP-1RAs during prepregnancy only, while 90 (64.3%) were exposed during pregnancy as well.

For the PGDM cohort, 175 unexposed controls were identified with 5 individuals classified as having type 1 diabetes mellitus and the remainder were type 2. For the WM cohort, random sampling yielded 200 controls (100 participants with BMI 30<40 kg/m2 and 100 BMI ≥40 kg/m2).

Table 1 characterizes GLP-1RA exposure separated by indication for medication use. In this cohort, the most common last GLP-1RA medication used prior to cessation for pregnancy was semaglutide (63.0%), followed by liraglutide (20.6%), dulaglutide (11.1%), tirzepatide (3.3%), and exenatide (2.1%). Most individuals were only exposed to one GLP-1RA medication (92.2%) during the study period. On average, GLP-1RA use was stopped 14.1 ± 115.4 days (median 30.0 days) prior to pregnancy, but this varied greatly by prepregnancy only exposure (−141.7 ± 105.5 days; median −113.0) compared with presence of some exposure during pregnancy (53.3 ± 36.3 days; median 45.0).

Overall, the data were complete with minimal missingness. Only 1 individual was missing the GWG variable in the PGDM cohort, and this individual was excluded from regression analysis evaluating the outcome of GWG. The WM cohort data collected were complete, and all other outcomes and covariates were complete.

Baseline clinical and demographic characteristics between GLP-1RA exposed and unexposed individuals are shown in Table 2. In the PGDM cohort, GLP-1RA exposed patients were more likely to be individuals of Black race, with pre-pregnancy BMI ≥30 kg/m2, and with a chronic hypertension diagnosis. The mean BMI for exposed individuals in the PGDM cohort was 38.7 ± 7.8 kg/m2 and for unexposed was 32.7 ± 7.8 kg/m2 (p<.001). The exposed and unexposed participants in the PGDM cohort did not differ by age, insurance status, parity, or PCOS diagnosis.

For the WM cohort, GLP-1RA exposed patients more frequently had PCOS and were less likely to have pre-pregnancy BMI ≥30 kg/m2 (Table 2). The mean BMI for exposed individuals in the WM cohort was 38.3 ± 8.1 kg/m2 and for unexposed was 39.9 ± 7.1 kg/m2 (p=0.06). The exposed and unexposed participants in the WM cohort did not differ by age, insurance status, parity, race and ethnicity, or chronic hypertension. Additional baseline clinical and demographic characteristics by timing of GLP-1RA exposure, HDP outcome, and GWG outcome are shown in Appendixes 2-4, available online at http://links.lww.com/xxx.

Primary and secondary obstetric outcomes are reported in Table 3. In the PGDM cohort, both crude and adjusted odds ratios showed that GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy was not associated with GWG above or below IOM recommendations (Table 4). Stratified multinomial modeling in the PGDM cohort demonstrated no association between GLP-1RA exposure during either prepregnancy only or during pregnancy periods and GWG.

In the WM cohort, GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of GWG below IOM recommendations in unadjusted analysis (OR= 0.44; 95% CI: 0.22-0.87) (Table 4). After adjusting for parity, HDP, and PCOS diagnosis, any GLP-1RA exposure (prepregnancy or pregnancy) in the WM cohort was associated with decreased odds of having GWG below IOM recommendations (aOR 0.38, 95% CI: 0.18-0.80). When stratified by timing of exposure, GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy was associated with decreased odds of GWG below IOM recommendations (aOR=0.29; 95% CI: 0.12-0.72), but prepregnancy only GLP-1RA exposure was not associated with GWG below IOM recommendations. Any GLP-1RA exposure in WM cohort was not associated with GWG that exceeded IOM recommendations (aOR=1.30; 95% CI: 0.69-2.44), and this was not changed when stratified by prepregnancy and pregnancy timing of exposure.

Results of crude and adjusted logistic regression models evaluating the outcome of HDP are shown in Table 5. In the PGDM cohort, GLP-1RA exposure was not associated with HDP (OR=0.63; 95% CI: 0.39-1.03) in crude models, yet the odds of HDP were reduced in multivariable analysis following adjustment for BMI, race and ethnicity, and cHTN diagnosis (aOR=0.52; 95% CI: 0.30-0.90). Stratified modeling by timing of exposure in the PGDM cohort showed GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy exposure was associated with lower odds of HDP after adjusting for pre-pregnancy BMI, race and ethnicity, cHTN diagnosis, and public insurance (aOR=0.52; 95% CI: 0.28-0.96). Prepregnancy only GLP-1RA exposure in the PGDM cohort was not associated with HDP in the adjusted model (aOR 0.51; 95% CI 0.21-1.14).

In the WM cohort, GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of HDP compared with unexposed in both crude (OR=0.51; 95% CI: 0.32-0.83) and multivariable analysis adjusted for parity, cHTN diagnosis, GDM, preterm birth, PCOS diagnosis, and maternal GWG (aOR=0.51; 95% CI: 0.30-0.87) (Table 5). When stratified by timing of GLP-1RA use in the WM cohort, GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy was associated with lower odds of developing HDP in both crude analysis (OR=0.51; 95% CI: 0.29-0.89) and after adjusting for parity, cHTN diagnosis, GDM, preterm birth, PCOS diagnosis, maternal GWG, and age (aOR=0.47; 95% CI: 0.25-0.89). Prepregnancy only GLP-1RA exposure in the WM cohort was not associated with HDP.

Regarding the secondary obstetric outcomes, unexposed patients in the PGDM cohort were more likely to be treated with metformin during pregnancy (Table 3). There was no difference by GLP-1RA exposure in PGDM groups for other secondary obstetric outcomes. For obstetric outcomes in the WM cohort, there were no differences between exposure status for secondary obstetric outcomes. Comparisons by GLP-1RA exposure status stratified by timing of exposure related to pregnancy (prepregnancy only vs during pregnancy) are shown in Appendix 5, while comparisons by outcomes of GWG and HDP are shown in Appendixes 6 and 7, available online at http://links.lww.com/xxx.

## Discussion:

This study found that peripregnancy GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of GWG below IOM recommendations when used for an indication of WM. GLP-1RA exposure up to one year before pregnancy was associated with lower odds of HDP in both individuals using GLP-1RA for PGDM and WM. These significant findings were driven primarily by GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy.

Our finding that peripregnancy GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of GWG below IOM recommendations in those using the medication for WM may reflect rebound weight gain after GLP-1RA cessation upon realization of pregnancy or during prepregnancy planning. This finding is consistent with the STEP-1 trial extension, which showed regain of two-thirds the weight lost in non-pregnant participants previously randomized to weekly semaglutide within one year after treatment withdrawal.24 Importantly, this trial showed substantial weight regain within the first 9 months of medication discontinuation, similar to the timeframe from GLP-1RA cessation to delivery in individuals with GLP-1RA exposure during pregnancy.24 While it may have been expected that those experiencing weight regain after treatment withdrawal would be more likely to experience GWG that exceeded IOM recommendations, studies showing weight regain after GLP-1RA treatment withdrawal still show overall net weight loss.24,25

The finding that peripregnancy GLP-1RA exposure was associated with lower odds of HDP in both individuals with PGDM and undergoing WM is consistent with non-pregnancy studies showing decreased cardiovascular risk, primarily myocardial infarction and cardiovascular-related death.12,13 In animal models, GLP-1RA medications have been shown to decrease circulation of IL-6, which has been shown to be elevated in plasma of human participants with preeclampsia.26 GLP-1RAs have also been shown to stimulate the cyclic AMP (cAMP) signaling pathway, which plays a role in trophoblast migration and invasion of the myometrium, and disruption of this pathway is involved in later preeclampsia development.27 Thus, a reduction in risk of HDP with GLP-1RA exposure during early pregnancy has biologic plausibility.

Despite this study’s potentially promising finding of an association between exposure and lower odds of HDP, the safety of GLP-1RAs during pregnancy has not been consistently demonstrated. Animal studies on GLP-1RAs during pregnancy have shown increased risk of embryonic death, growth restriction, and visceral and skeletal malformations.7 Reassuringly, case reports of first trimester GLP-1RA use in humans have not demonstrated these adverse outcomes in offspring.7,9

One human randomized controlled trial (RCT) followed 176 patients with PCOS, elevated BMI, and infertility and randomized participants to exenatide or metformin for 12 weeks followed by both groups taking metformin until pregnancy.28 Consistent with our study, no differences were noted in preterm birth, GDM, and birthweight.5,28 In contrast to our study, no significant differences were found in incidence of gHTN or GWG. This difference may be explained by this RCT not continuing GLP-1RA use after pregnancy fertilization and defining outcomes differently (GWG not accounting for gestational age at delivery and gHTN abstracted alone rather than all HDPs). Lastly, only 5 (2.1%) individuals in our study had last GLP-1RA exposure of exenatide and the remaining had exposure to newer, more effective GLP-1RAs.27

This retrospective cohort study was limited by its observational nature and possibility of residual confounding. Small sample sizes limited the power to detect potentially meaningful clinical differences. While the EMR query with manual abstraction to confirm GLP-1RA exposure was performed meticulously, patients may have obtained GLP-1RAs from other sources not identified by EMR prescription data, such as compounded GLP-1RAs available direct to consumer. This study did not account for the effect of glycemic control during pregnancy or medication-associated weight loss on pregnancy outcomes, which may be important when considering patients with PGDM. Several variables, most importantly HDP as well as diagnoses of PCOS, cHTN, and FGR, were identified via ICD-10 codes, which are prone to misclassification. History of bariatric surgery was also not available in this data repository. Additionally, the exposure variable included any GLP-1RA, grouping older agents, such as exenatide, dulaglutide, and liraglutide, with newer, more effective agents, such as semaglutide, which was most prevalent, and the dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor co-agonist tirzepatide.

Strengths include manual abstraction of many variables including verification of exposure to GLP-1RA and end date of medication use. Manual abstraction was also used to limit missingness. Moreover, a highly curated database was used to extract several key variables for analysis, enabling accurate data collection. Lastly, we had separation of outcomes by timing of GLP-1RA use as prepregnancy or during early pregnancy and indication for medication use, highlighting different possible interventional approaches and target populations.

Overall, this study provides novel data on obstetric outcomes following GLP-1RA exposure up to one year prior to pregnancy. The observed associations with lower odds of GWG below IOM recommendations and HDP were most pronounced with exposure during early pregnancy. Future studies are needed to determine whether pregnancy outcomes are improved with GLP-1RA exposure itself or due to associated weight loss with their use. In addition, larger cohorts are needed to evaluate safety of these medications in pregnancy.
